paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Ἱππίας εἰς τὰς Ἀθήνας ἥκει καὶ Σωκράτει διαλέγεται. θαυμάζει ὅτι ὁ Σωκράτης ἔτι περὶ τῶν αὐτῶν λέγει. ὁ δὲ οὐκ αἰσχύνεται ταὐτὰ ζητῶν· οὐ γὰρ τὸ καινὸν μόνον ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀληθὲς σκοπεῖ. ὁ Ἱππίας ἀξιοῖ αὐτὸν μὴ μόνον τοὺς ἄλλους ἐρωτᾶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γνώμην περὶ δικαιοσύνης εἰπεῖν.

Ὁ Σωκράτης πρῶτον τὸν βίον αὑτοῦ παράδειγμα παρέχει. οὐ ψευδῆ μαρτυρεῖ οὐδὲ τοὺς φίλους εἰς στάσιν ἄγει. ὁ δὲ Ἱππίας λόγον σαφέστερον ζητεῖ· οὐ γὰρ ἀρκεῖ λέγειν ἃ ὁ δίκαιος οὐ ποιεῖ. τί οὖν ποιεῖ; ὁ Σωκράτης τὸ νόμιμον δίκαιον εἶναί φησιν. οὕτως ἐκ τῶν ἔργων εἰς τὸν ὁρισμὸν ὁ λόγος μεταβαίνει.

Ὁ Ἱππίας ἐρωτᾷ πῶς τοῦτο λέγει. οἱ γὰρ πολῖται τοὺς νόμους τίθενται, ἔπειτα δὲ μεταβάλλουσιν. πῶς οὖν τοῖς νόμοις πιστεύωμεν, ὅταν οἱ θέμενοι αὐτοὶ μὴ μένωσιν ἐν τοῖς αὐτοῖς; ἡ ἐρώτησις οὐ μικρά ἐστιν. ἄλλο γάρ ἐστι νόμῳ πείθεσθαι, ἄλλο δὲ τὸν νόμον ἀεὶ βέλτιστον νομίζειν. τὴν διαφορὰν ταύτην ὁ ἀναγνώστης ἐξετάζει.

Ὁ Σωκράτης τὴν εὐνομίαν ἐπαινεῖ. οἱ γὰρ νόμοι τοὺς πολίτας πρὸς κοινὰ ἔργα συνάγουσιν, καὶ ἡ ὁμόνοια τὴν πόλιν ἰσχυροτέραν ποιεῖ. οὐ μόνον δὲ περὶ τῶν γεγραμμένων λέγει· ἐρωτᾷ καὶ περὶ ἀγράφων νόμων. τὸ τοὺς γονέας τιμᾶν καὶ τὸ χάριν ἀποδιδόναι παραδείγματα παρέχει. τούτους τοὺς νόμους πρὸς τοὺς θεοὺς ἀναφέρει.

Νῦν ἡμεῖς τὸν λόγον ἐξετάζοντες εὐχὰς καὶ δυνατὰ λέγομεν. εἴθε οἱ πολῖται δικαίως κρίνοιεν. εἴθε μὴ τὸ κέρδος τοῦ δικαίου προτιμῷεν. ὁ δίκαιος ἀνὴρ οὐχ ἁπλῶς τῷ ἰσχυρῷ πείθοιτο ἄν· πρῶτον γὰρ τὸ κελευόμενον ἐξετάζοι ἄν. οὐ λέγομεν ὅτι πάντα ταῦτα γίγνεται, ἀλλὰ τί εὐχόμεθα καὶ τί δυνατὸν εἶναι νομίζομεν.

Ἡ περὶ δικαιοσύνης ζήτησις οὐ τελευτᾷ ἑνὶ λόγῳ. ὁ ἀναγνώστης μνημονεύει τοῦ Σωκράτους πρὸς τὴν ἄνομον ψῆφον ἀντειπόντος. ἐκεῖνος νόμῳ βοηθεῖν ἐβούλετο, οὐ τῇ τῶν πολλῶν ὀργῇ. νόμος δὲ καὶ τὸ ὑπὸ δυνατοῦ ἀνδρὸς κελευόμενον οὐκ ἀεὶ ταὐτόν ἐστιν. τοῦτο σκοποῖμεν ἄν, ἵνα μὴ τὴν τῆς πόλεως δύναμιν ἄνευ κρίσεως ἐπαινῶμεν.

reading.translation:
Hippias arrives in Athens and converses with Socrates. He is surprised that Socrates still speaks about the same things. Socrates is not ashamed of investigating the same matters; he considers not only what is new but what is true. Hippias asks him not merely to question others but to state his own view about justice.

Socrates first offers his own life as an example. He does not give false testimony or lead friends into faction. Hippias seeks a clearer explanation: it is not enough to say what the just person does not do. What, then, does he do? Socrates says that what is lawful is just. Thus the argument moves from actions to a definition.

Hippias asks how he can say this. Citizens establish laws and then change them. How, then, should we trust laws whenever those who established them do not themselves remain with the same rules? The question is substantial. Obeying a law is one thing, considering it always the best another. The reader examines this distinction.

Socrates praises good order under law. Laws bring citizens together for common tasks, and concord makes the city stronger. He speaks not only about written rules; he also asks about unwritten laws. He offers honoring parents and returning kindness as examples. He refers these laws to the gods.

Now, in examining the argument, we express wishes and possibilities. May the citizens judge justly. May they not prefer gain to justice. A just person might not simply obey the powerful; he might first examine the command. We are not saying that all this happens, but what we wish and what we consider possible.

The inquiry about justice does not end with a single statement. The reader remembers Socrates objecting to the unlawful vote. He wished to defend law, not the anger of the majority. Law and what a powerful man commands are not always the same. We might examine this so that we do not praise the city’s power without judgment.

sections.title: 1. Present and aorist active optatives
body: The optative presents wishes, possibilities, and certain subordinate reports or general situations. Regular present active forms are λύοιμι, λύοις, λύοι, λύοιμεν, λύοιτε, λύοιεν. The οι is a useful clue, but not every οι in a word marks an optative. Compare indicative λύει and optative λύοι.

First aorist active forms include λύσαιμι, λύσαις/λύσειας, λύσαι/λύσειε(ν), λύσαιμεν, λύσαιτε, λύσαιεν/λύσειαν. A second aorist uses its stem: λάβοιμι. No augment appears. Present versus aorist expresses aspect outside oblique reporting, not a simple present-versus-past time opposition.

sections.title: 2. Middle, passive, and contract optatives
body: Present middle/passive forms are λυοίμην, λύοιο, λύοιτο, λυοίμεθα, λύοισθε, λύοιντο. First aorist middle forms are λυσαίμην, λύσαιο, λύσαιτο, λυσαίμεθα, λύσαισθε, λύσαιντο. Aorist passive uses -ειη- in the singular, as λυθείην, λυθείης, λυθείη; plural λυθεῖμεν, λυθεῖτε, λυθεῖεν has shorter alternatives beside longer forms.

Contract verbs combine stem vowels with optative vowels. Learn τιμῴην/τιμῷμι, ποιοίην/ποιοῖμι and their common plurals τιμῷμεν, ποιοῖμεν. εἰμί has εἴην, εἴης, εἴη, εἶμεν/εἴημεν, εἶτε/εἴητε, εἶεν/εἴησαν. Use a reference table when recognizing alternative forms.

sections.title: 3. Wishes and potentiality
body: A wish for the future can use the optative alone or with εἴθε/εἰ γάρ: εἴθε δικαίως κρίνοιεν, “May they judge justly.” Negate such a wish with μή. This is an aspiration, not a claim that the action has occurred.

Potential optative normally has ἄν: δικαίως κρίνοιεν ἄν, “They might judge justly” or “They would judge justly,” depending on context. Negation is normally οὐ. The particle belongs to the potential statement, not to an ordinary wish. Translate the speaker’s degree of commitment before assigning an English modal.

sections.title: 4. Optatives in subordinate clauses
body: After a historical main verb, a purpose, fear, or finite report may shift to the optative: ἐδίδασκεν ἵνα μάθοι, “He taught so that the pupil might learn.” The optative is not a new main-clause wish merely because its ending resembles one. Retaining a subjunctive or indicative can also be possible, depending on the original construction.

In a finite report, the optative can represent the original speaker’s mood and tense from the narrator’s historical viewpoint. Compare λέγει ὅτι δίκαιός ἐστι with ἔλεγεν ὅτι δίκαιος εἴη. We develop athematic forms and indirect questions next. Do not place potential ἄν into every subordinate optative.

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Memorabilia
body: Book 4, chapter 4 puts a definition under pressure. Hippias asks Socrates to state a position about justice, and the discussion moves from conduct to law and unwritten obligations. The lesson asks you to reconstruct the argument fairly before judging it. A defense of Socrates can preserve a challenging objection as well as a confident response.

Think of the four books as a gallery of encounters rather than a continuous biography. Book 1 answers accusations against Socrates and presents his religious practice and daily conduct. Books 2–3 explore family, friendship, useful work, and leadership. Book 4 gives sustained attention to education, including the questioning of Euthydemus. The movement from an ordinary habit to a public responsibility is characteristic of the collection.

Xenophon writes as an advocate for a teacher condemned at Athens in 399 BCE. His Socrates improves other people through example, questions, and practical reasoning. That organizing purpose makes the work valuable evidence for an ancient interpretation of Socrates; it does not make every conversation a stenographic record. Notice who asks the questions, who changes position, and where the narrator supplies the judgment.

Reading invitation: open Book 1, chapter 5, then Book 4, chapter 5. Ask whether mastery of appetite is merely a rule about pleasure or a condition for learning and dependable action. Keep a small dossier of the different kinds of evidence Xenophon offers: reported speech, observed habit, analogy, and the narrator’s praise.
Track Hippias’s objections as carefully as Socrates’ answers, and identify what each successive example contributes to the definition.

sections.title: A definition under pressure
body: Hippias challenges Socrates to state what justice is rather than only question other people. Socrates points to conduct and then connects the just with the lawful. Hippias’ objection that laws change is an important part of the conversation, not an interruption to be skipped on the way to a slogan.

Distinguish three claims: that a city needs law, that citizens should obey law, and that every existing law is morally best. They are not interchangeable. Read Socrates’ reasons and Hippias’ objections before deciding how far the argument succeeds.

sections.title: Unwritten laws
body: The dialogue extends beyond written civic rules to obligations described as unwritten, including honoring parents and returning benefits. Socrates relates these to divine authority. Their universality is a claim made in the discussion, not a conclusion independently established about every human society.

Compare an inscription, a customary expectation, and a claim about divine law. They have different kinds of authority and different ways of being challenged. The banner’s inscribed surface is a reconstruction without a fabricated readable ancient law; use the actual literary passage for the words being interpreted.

sections.title: Return to Socrates’ refusal
body: Revisit Lesson 40. Socrates’ resistance to a collective vote appeals to lawful procedure against immediate pressure. How does that example bear on the claim that lawful conduct is just? Explain a possible connection without pretending the two passages settle every problem about unjust laws.

Translate the dialogue’s objection before its response. Then distinguish the course’s optative wishes from its potential statements. Write a wish for fair judgment and a possibility about what a citizen might do, and explain why neither is evidence that the action actually occurred.
